claims.text: The as-deposited protective coating has a mixed FCC/BCC microstructure.
The as-deposited coating contains a controlled distribution of fine phase boundaries.
Cooling rate and post-deposition heat treatment can systematically vary FCC/BCC phase-boundary density without changing overall alloy composition.
The relevant loading regime is at intermediate temperatures where dislocation-based plasticity dominates and diffusional creep is minimal.
FCC/BCC interfaces are the structural mediator governing creep resistance.
Increasing FCC/BCC phase-boundary density impedes dislocation motion during continuous loading.
Phase boundaries obstruct dislocations by causing pile-ups or forcing changes in deformation mechanism.
Obstruction of dislocation motion by phase boundaries reduces the creep-deformation rate under sustained stress.
Coatings with higher phase-boundary density will develop less cumulative strain over time than coatings with lower phase-boundary density.
Coatings with higher phase-boundary density will have a lower creep rate than coatings with lower phase-boundary density.
The phase-boundary mechanism is expected to operate under intermediate-temperature and intermediate-stress conditions typical of protective coatings.
The mechanism may cease to govern at temperatures high enough for diffusional creep.
The mechanism may not apply at stresses too low to activate dislocation motion.
Prior evidence supports a relationship between phase-boundary density and creep rate.
The quantitative magnitude and loading-condition dependence of the proposed effect are uncertain.

The hypothesis is falsified if higher-boundary-density coatings show no statistically significant creep-rate reduction relative to both the baseline and low-boundary-density coatings, or if boundary density does not correlate with creep resistance.
